A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FastForward research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across reordered sections.

before.justification: V1 reports original FastForward localization results, scale-normalization and map-representation ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative examples.

after.justification: V2 retains original FastForward experiments and reports additional comparator evaluations and an E5+1 accuracy–latency study.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same encoder, decoders, prediction heads, feature sampling, ray encoding, scale normalization, and training loss. The changed PnP correspondence budget is an experimental setting revision, without a new model component or localization algorithm.

E1.justification: The training dataset mixture and evaluation coverage remain unchanged: Cambridge, Wayspots, Indoor6, RIO10, 7-Scenes, and Map-free validation analyses. Additional baseline configurations and acceptance thresholds do not introduce new datasets or task scenarios.

E2.justification: V2 adds E5+1 with ALIKED-LightGlue to comparisons on all five localization benchmarks and E5+1 with RoMa on Wayspots. These introduce a substantive geometric comparator family absent from v1's evaluations; existing benchmark competitors are retained.

E3.justification: Section 4 changes the stated PnP correspondence maximum from 100,000 to 5,000. Figures 4–5 add a 25cm/5° acceptance threshold, and Appendix C.6 introduces keypoint-count and RANSAC-budget sweeps. Existing training budgets and dataset splits remain unchanged. V2 Appendix A's 'at least 5,000' wording leaves the precise subsampling rule unclear.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.6 and Table 10 systematically test the strongest added comparator's accuracy–latency trade-off on Cambridge and Wayspots by varying keypoints and RANSAC iterations. This adds a substantive comparative sensitivity analysis. Existing scale, retrieval, feature-count, and MASt3R analyses remain, with Figures 4–5 extended to another acceptance threshold.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for the empirical results. The model's predicted confidence scores and confidence-based loss are unchanged.

E6.justification: New comparator results alter rankings: v2 Table 4 reports Cambridge errors of 0.18m/0.3° for E5+1 versus FastForward's retained 0.27m/0.4°. Existing FastForward accuracies are revised, including Wayspots 51.0% to 51.4% and RIO10 44.6% to 40.6% at 10cm/10°. Appendix C.3 changes reported network/PnP times from 0.6/2.2 seconds to 0.4/0.1 seconds. These revisions accompany a changed correspondence budget and do not establish controlled same-setting gains. V1's per-scene Cambridge threshold-accuracy breakdown is removed.

T1.justification: The normalization definitions, ray encoding, decoder equations, and confidence-weighted loss are unchanged. The added E5+1 discussion explains an existing geometric solver without introducing new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: sparse mapping features enable feed-forward localization with minimal map preparation, and scene/scale normalization supports generalization. Benchmark-specific ranking revisions do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies practical applicability. Section 4.5 discusses amortizing mapping costs over repeated queries; Appendix B.1 explains storage disadvantages relative to SCR. The benchmark discussion and Appendix C.6 explain when geometric matching excels or fails. Appendix B.2 also interprets existing results in terms of imperfect SLAM poses and retrieval failures, without adding dedicated tests of those conditions.

D1.justification: V2 adds ALIKED-LightGlue resolution/keypoint settings, E5+1 RANSAC budgets, storage requirements, and Wayspots pose-provenance details. Core training hyperparameters and hardware remain unchanged. V1's supplementary-video access instructions are omitted, although the project link remains; this does not establish that the videos became unavailable.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantive positioning against semi-generalized relative-pose methods, including their ability to recover absolute scale from posed mapping images. It also discusses retrieval-based local triangulation and Viewformer, with supporting citations. This expands the relevant research context beyond v1's emphasis on regression and foundation-model approaches.

P1.justification: V2 tightens introductory prose, moves Cambridge from Section 4.1 to 4.4, adds focused discussion and Appendix C.6, and changes the publication header. Most method exposition, the abstract, and the conclusion remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are substantially reorganized: Wayspots accuracies move from appendix Table 6 into main-text Table 2, replacing the Cambridge accuracy table. Several tables gain comparator rows and latency/storage columns, and Table 10 is new. Figures 4–5 have expanded curves, axes, and legends; the architecture and qualitative figures are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important comparison gap by evaluating relevant multi-view geometric baselines, acknowledging their wins on Cambridge and the strict 7-Scenes threshold, and examining their accuracy–latency trade-offs. The added amortization and storage discussion makes the central efficiency argument more credible and useful. These gains outweigh the loss of Cambridge's per-scene threshold breakdown and remaining ambiguity in the 5,000-correspondence wording.
